passages.text: As companies in several countries experiment with a four-day week, the two-day weekend feels so inevitable that it is easy to forget how recent an invention it is. In nineteenth-century Britain, many craftsmen habitually skipped work on Mondays, a custom facetiously dubbed Saint Monday, to recuperate from their Sunday carousing. Employers, eager for a more dependable workforce, grudgingly conceded a Saturday half-holiday in exchange for punctual attendance at the start of the week. In the United States, Henry Ford granted his assembly-line workers a five-day week in 1926, reasoning that people with leisure time would purchase more cars and other goods. The weekend, in other words, was not a pure gift of munificence but the product of ____ between workers and employers.

Plants cannot flee from the insects that eat them, but a growing body of research suggests that they are far from defenseless. When caterpillars begin gnawing on a leaf, many plants emit a cloud of volatile chemicals, and neighboring plants that perceive these compounds start synthesizing bitter toxins before the insects ever reach them. Some species even lure parasitic wasps that deposit their eggs inside the caterpillars. In effect, a wounded plant sounds an alarm, giving neighboring plants time to <u>bolster</u> their defenses.

In a renowned experiment, researchers presented volunteers with pairs of photographs of faces and asked them to pick the more appealing one. The experimenter then handed over the chosen photo for closer scrutiny, except that, through a deft sleight of hand, it was sometimes the face the volunteer had (A) ____. Remarkably, most people were oblivious to the switch. More astonishing still, they went on to justify why they had preferred that face, citing features such as earrings that were present only in the photo they had not picked. The finding implies that the reasons we give for our choices are often (B) ____ after the fact rather than the true causes of our decisions.

For centuries, painters ground their own pigments and mixed them with oil in the studio, storing the paste in animal bladders that were prone to burst. In 1841 the American portrait painter John Goffe Rand patented a Ⓐ<u>collapsible</u> metal tube that kept paint moist and could be sealed with a cap. The invention seems unremarkable, yet it Ⓑ<u>transformed</u> the practice of art. Liberated from the studio, artists could transport dozens of hues into fields and along riverbanks and paint directly from nature. The Impressionists, who strove to capture transient light in a few hours outdoors, relied heavily on this Ⓒ<u>cumbersome</u> new convenience. A modest technical innovation thus helped make possible a movement that would Ⓓ<u>reshape</u> modern painting.

The fourteenth-century English friar William of Ockham is remembered today principally for a principle that bears his name, though he never articulated it in its modern form. Occam's razor counsels that, when two explanations account for the same data equally well, we should prefer the one that requires fewer postulates. The principle does not assert that the most economical theory is always true; nature is under no obligation to be tidy. Rather, it is a ____ guide: it tells inquirers where to begin, not where they must end.

When chatbots adept at composing fluent essays became widely accessible in late 2022, many schools reacted with consternation. New York City's public school system, the largest in the United States, blocked access to one prominent chatbot on its networks in early 2023, only to lift the ban a few months later. Teachers who had hoped that detection software would catch machine-written homework were also disillusioned. Such tools frequently misattributed students' own writing to machines, and in 2023 one major AI developer shelved its own detector, citing its dismal accuracy. Many educators have since redirected their attention from catching students to overhauling assignments; some require drafts written in class, oral defenses of written work, or candid reflections on how an AI tool was used. Others contend that schools should teach students to scrutinize chatbot answers, which can sound authoritative while being entirely ____.

The phrase Silk Road <u>conjures up</u> images of a single highway along which camel caravans plodded from China to Rome. The reality was far more haphazard, and the term itself was coined only in 1877 by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen, long after the trade it describes had waned. What it actually denoted was a protean web of routes across deserts, mountains and seas, and few merchants ever traversed its full length. Instead, goods passed from hand to hand through a chain of intermediaries, each exacting a profit before selling them on. Silk was only one of myriad commodities. Creeds, technologies and pathogens migrated along these paths too, and their influence often proved far more enduring than that of any bale of cloth.

Ice shelves are floating platforms of ice tethered to the Antarctic coast, replenished by glaciers that flow down from the interior. Because they are already buoyant, their melting does not directly raise sea levels, much as melting ice cubes do not make a glass overflow. Their significance lies elsewhere: they act as a (A) ____, holding back the glaciers behind them. When the Larsen B ice shelf disintegrated within a few weeks in 2002, the glaciers it had restrained began sliding seaward several times faster than before. Icebergs break off from shelves spontaneously, sometimes on a colossal scale: the iceberg known as A23a calved from the Filchner Ice Shelf in 1986 and remained lodged on the seafloor for more than three decades before finally drifting away in recent years. Glaciologists caution that a single iceberg reveals little in isolation; what (B) ____ them is the inexorable thinning of the shelves.

"Again," said Mr. Oh, nudging a fresh bowl of flour across the steel table. It was nearly three in the morning, and I had just <u>botched</u> an entire batch of rolls by forgetting the salt. I had taken the night shift at the bakery near the bus terminal imagining something idyllic: warm ovens, the aroma of bread, the city slumbering outside. Instead, my first week was a tedious blur of scrubbing trays and scorching my wrists on racks I had been cautioned twice not to touch. The head baker was famously taciturn and I had braced myself for a tirade, yet he offered nothing but that single word. Within a few months I could shape a hundred rolls an hour. What lingers in my memory, though, is not the skill but the quiet dignity of being trusted with a second chance.

Tulip mania, the speculative frenzy that gripped the Dutch Republic in the 1630s, is often invoked as the first great financial bubble. In the conventional telling, prices for rare bulbs skyrocketed until a single bulb could fetch the price of a house. Then they plummeted overnight in early 1637, impoverishing thousands of families and plunging the nation into despair. The historian Anne Goldgar, who scrutinized contracts and court records for a widely reviewed 2007 book, paints a far more <u>sober</u> picture. She found that comparatively few buyers were gravely harmed, that much of the trading involved affluent merchants who could weather their losses, and that the wider Dutch economy continued to flourish. The more lurid version, she argues, owes much to moralizing pamphlets disseminated after the crash, which exploited the episode to condemn greed.

Every new medium seems to arrive with a chorus of censure, and in the eighteenth century the culprit was the novel. Clergymen, physicians, and essayists admonished readers that prose fiction would (A) ____ young readers, especially young women, filling their heads with fanciful expectations of love and leaving them unfit for the duties of quotidian life. Some critics described compulsive novel reading almost as an affliction, lamenting that readers lost track of time, neglected their families, and stayed up by candlelight to finish one more chapter.
To modern ears, these complaints sound faintly risible. The novel is now taught in schools as a cornerstone of literary culture, and parents who once would have confiscated a romance now fret that their children read too few books. Yet the structure of the old argument has proved remarkably <u>durable</u>. Radio, television and smartphones have each been indicted for the same crimes: monopolizing attention, corrupting morals, and alienating the young from real life.
None of this demonstrates that every worry about new technology is misplaced; some concerns have proved warranted. But history counsels a measure of humility: the dire predictions of moral ruin made about earlier media were largely (B) ____, and we would do well to scrutinize the evidence before repeating them.

Many Roman harbors, aqueducts, and domes have endured for two millennia, while some modern concrete structures begin to deteriorate within decades. A study published in 2023 by a team led by researchers at MIT furnished one explanation. Roman builders appear to have mixed their concrete using quicklime, a technique that left small white clumps of lime dispersed through the material. Long dismissed as a sign of negligent mixing, these lumps may in fact have been the secret of its longevity. When cracks formed and water seeped in, the lime dissolved and recrystallized, ____ the cracks before they could spread.

When people look back on a distressing experience, they do not simply tally every moment of discomfort. In one experiment, participants held a hand in very cold water for sixty seconds in one trial; in another, they endured the same sixty seconds followed by thirty more in water that was marginally less frigid. Asked which trial they would rather repeat, most chose the longer one, even though it involved more cumulative pain. Psychologists account for this with the peak-end rule: our memory of an experience is shaped largely by its most intense moment and by ____.

In the hot summer of 1858, the stench rising from the River Thames became so overpowering that members of Parliament hung curtains saturated with chloride of lime over their windows in a bid to ward it off. For decades, London's sewage had been discharged straight into the river that also supplied much of the city's drinking water. What finally <u>spurred</u> action was not the cholera outbreaks that had already killed thousands but the discomfort of the lawmakers themselves. Within weeks, Parliament sanctioned funding for an immense network of sewers designed by the engineer Joseph Bazalgette.

The anthropologist Robin Dunbar posited in the 1990s that humans can sustain stable relationships with only about 150 people. He predicated this figure on a (A) ____ between brain size and group size in primates: species with a larger neocortex tend to live in larger social groups. Dunbar observed that the number recurs in many human settings, from the size of Neolithic villages to that of military companies. Critics contend that the estimate rests on tenuous statistical assumptions and that the real limit may fluctuate widely from person to person. Social media, with its thousands of friends and followers, has not demonstrably (B) ____ the limit, since most users converse regularly with only a small circle.

The Dutch painter Johannes Vermeer bequeathed to posterity fewer than forty paintings and scant written records, which has made his methods a subject of lasting Ⓐ<u>speculation</u>. Some researchers have contended that he used a camera obscura, a darkened box that projects an image through a lens, to help compose his scenes. They point to the Ⓑ<u>photographic</u> qualities of his work, such as blurred highlights that mimic the effects of an out-of-focus lens. Skeptics insist that the evidence is Ⓒ<u>conclusive</u> and that Vermeer's precision attests to nothing more than extraordinary virtuosity and patience. Because no sketches or notes survive, the debate is unlikely ever to be fully Ⓓ<u>settled</u>.

On La Gomera, one of the Canary Islands, precipitous ravines once made travel between villages slow and <u>arduous</u>, and long before telephones arrived, islanders devised a means of sending messages across these chasms: a whistled form of Spanish known as Silbo Gomero. By modulating the pitch and duration of their whistles, adept speakers can convey words and whole sentences over distances of several kilometers. When the practice began to wane in the twentieth century, the island's government made it a mandatory subject in local schools, and in 2009 UNESCO inscribed it as part of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity.

Scroll through any popular social media feed and it can be hard to discern where personal recommendation ends and advertising begins. When an influencer extols a skin cream, followers may presume the enthusiasm is (A) ____, unaware that the post was underwritten by the manufacturer. Regulators in many countries have responded by stiffening disclosure requirements. In the United States, the Federal Trade Commission revised its guidance on endorsements in 2023, underscoring that a paid relationship must be disclosed conspicuously rather than obscured among dozens of hashtags. South Korea's competition authority had already instituted similar rules in 2020 after a spate of undisclosed sponsorships.
Enforcement, however, remains (B) ____. Myriad posts appear daily, and many smaller creators remain oblivious to the fact that the rules apply to them.

Imagine you are asked to devise the rules of a society, with one condition: you will not know in advance what position you will occupy in it. You might be born affluent or destitute, robust or infirm, gifted or mediocre. The philosopher John Rawls, who propounded this thought experiment in his 1971 book A Theory of Justice, dubbed this condition the veil of ignorance. Behind the veil, he contended, prudent people would not gamble on being among the privileged. Instead, they would opt for rules that safeguard the worst-off, since any one of them might end up there. The experiment is meant to <u>strip away</u> self-interest, compelling us to judge institutions from a standpoint that is genuinely impartial.

For most animals, sleep is a perilous necessity: a sleeping creature cannot scan for predators. Some species have found an ingenious (A) ____. Dolphins, seals, and many birds can sleep with one half of the brain at a time while the other half stays vigilant, and the eye governed by the waking half often remains open. Ducks roosting at the periphery of a group have been observed keeping their outward-facing eye open, as if posting a sentinel. In 2016 researchers who affixed recording devices to frigatebirds found that these seabirds sleep while flying, often in bursts of only a few seconds and mostly with one hemisphere. Over a day aloft, the birds slept far (B) ____ than they did on land.

For decades, most economists presumed that raising the minimum wage would inevitably cost jobs: if labor becomes more costly, employers will hire fewer workers. In 1992, however, New Jersey raised its minimum wage while neighboring Pennsylvania did not, creating what economists term a natural experiment. David Card and Alan Krueger canvassed hundreds of fast-food restaurants on both sides of the state line and found no evidence that employment declined in New Jersey relative to Pennsylvania. Their study provoked <u>vehement</u> criticism and protracted debate, but it also helped popularize a style of economics that tests theories against real-world data rather than relying on abstract models alone. In 2021, Card shared the Nobel Prize in economics partly for this research.

By the time the last ferry pulled away from the island, the rain had turned to sleet, and Hana discovered she had left her coat in the café on the pier. She stood at the rail, arms folded, trying to appear as though the cold did not bother her. A grizzled man in a fisherman's cap regarded her for a while, then without a word shed his heavy wool jacket and draped it over her shoulders. She demurred, but he only shrugged and gestured at the thick sweater he wore underneath. For forty minutes they stood side by side in companionable silence. When the ferry docked, she turned to return the jacket, but he had already <u>melted into</u> the crowd jostling down the ramp. She kept the jacket for years, cherishing a stranger's wordless kindness.

In 2018 Britain became the first country to appoint a minister for loneliness, and Japan followed in 2021, establishing a similar post as reports of isolation proliferated during the pandemic. In 2023 the United States Surgeon General issued an advisory characterizing loneliness as an epidemic, likening its effect on mortality to that of smoking up to fifteen cigarettes a day. Japan went further still in April 2024, when a law obliging national and local governments to combat loneliness and isolation took effect. Skeptics question whether governments can ____ something as intimate as friendship. Proponents counter that the state already molds social life through the design of housing, transport, and public spaces, and that loneliness imposes tangible costs on health systems.

Long before commercial yeast was marketed in packets, bakers leavened their bread with a sourdough starter, a rudimentary mixture of flour and water left to ferment. A 2020 study comparing starters from bakers on several continents suggested that such a starter captures wild yeasts and bacteria from the flour, the air, and even the baker's own hands. The yeasts produce carbon dioxide, which makes the dough rise, while lactic acid bacteria generate the acids that impart to the bread its tangy flavor. Because these microbial communities differ markedly from bakery to bakery, a starter nurtured for decades in one bakery can produce bread with a taste that is ____.

In his autobiography, Benjamin Franklin recounts how he won over a rival legislator who had obstructed him. Instead of flattering the man, Franklin asked to (A) ____ a rare book from his library. The rival agreed, Franklin returned it with a note of thanks, and the two became steadfast friends. Psychologists have since proffered an explanation for this paradoxical result. Having done Franklin a favor, the rival felt compelled to justify his own conduct, and the most expedient way to do so was to deduce that Franklin must be worthy of assistance. In other words, we tend to (B) ____ the people we have helped, not only help the people we like.

In the 1790s, long before the electric telegraph, the French engineer Claude Chappe erected a network of towers that could relay messages across the country in a matter of hours. Each tower carried a set of movable wooden arms whose positions signified letters, numbers, or whole phrases. An operator peering at the next tower through a telescope would Ⓐ<u>copy</u> each signal and transmit it down the line. The system was remarkably expeditious, but it had conspicuous Ⓑ<u>limitations</u>: it could not work at night or in fog, and it demanded a large cadre of trained staff. The French government used it predominantly for military and official messages, keeping its codes Ⓒ<u>public</u>. By the 1850s, however, the electric telegraph rendered the towers Ⓓ<u>obsolete</u>.

The haiku is a short Japanese poem traditionally arranged in three phrases of five, seven and five sound units. It may seem too <u>terse</u> to say anything of consequence; its potency, however, lies precisely in what it omits. The seventeenth-century master Matsuo Bashō often presented a solitary concrete image such as a frog leaping into an old pond, and he trusted readers to supply the feeling it evoked. A good haiku does not explain; it suggests, beckoning the reader to complete the poem in imagination.

As regulators debate how far to trust the benchmark scores that AI companies publish for their models, an old warning from economics is back in vogue. In 1975 the British economist Charles Goodhart observed that statistical indicators tend to lose their validity once governments endeavor to control them, an insight that has since been extended far beyond economics. When hospitals are assessed by waiting times, some may contrive ways to keep patients off the official list; when schools are ranked by test scores, teachers may spend more time drilling for exams than instructing. In each case, a number that once offered a serviceable gauge of reality becomes ____ as soon as people are rewarded for changing it.

Bullying once ceased, at least for a while, when a child left the schoolyard. Smartphones have upended that. Insults and humiliating images can now follow young people home and circulate among hundreds of classmates within minutes, and the anonymity of some platforms can <u>embolden</u> attackers. Legislators have scrambled to keep pace: many countries have amended their laws so that schools must intervene in online harassment, and some have made intimidating or abusive messages a criminal offense. In late 2024 Australia went further, enacting a law that requires major social media platforms to bar children under sixteen from holding accounts, with the rules taking effect in December 2025. Proponents laud the ban as long-overdue protection. Critics contend that it may inadvertently shunt teenagers toward murkier corners of the internet, where harassment is even harder to monitor.

Every autumn, millions of songbirds migrate thousands of kilometers to wintering grounds they may never have seen, often journeying by night. How they navigate has long puzzled biologists: birds are known to exploit the position of the sun and the constellations, but they also appear to sense the Earth's magnetic field. One prominent hypothesis posits that proteins called cryptochromes in birds' eyes react to magnetism, conceivably allowing the animals to perceive the field as a faint pattern superimposed on their vision. Experiments with European robins have <u>lent weight to</u> this idea: in the laboratory, feeble radio-frequency noise appears to disrupt their orientation. If confirmed, the hypothesis would mean that birds can, in a sense, see a force that is invisible to us.

Dear Mina,
You asked in your last letter whether I rue leaving the city to keep the lighthouse on this island. The candid answer is that I did, for the whole of the first winter. The wind was relentless, the supply boat called only twice a month, and the silence at night was so absolute that I could hear my own heartbeat. But in spring, something in me thawed. I began to discern the birds that roosted on the precipitous cliffs, then the capricious moods of the sea, then the faint creaks the old tower makes as it cools after sunset. I no longer tally the days until the boat arrives. I think I have learned, at last, to be ____ without being lonely. Write soon, and tell me everything about your new apartment.
Your brother, Joon

Zero seems so self-evident to us that it is hard to conceive of arithmetic without it. Yet many sophisticated ancient civilizations dispensed with a true zero. The Babylonians eventually employed a placeholder symbol to denote a vacant position in a number, but they did not treat zero as a number in its own right. That (A) ____ came in India. In 628 the mathematician Brahmagupta formulated rules for computing with zero, asserting for example that a number minus itself equals zero. Indian numerals, including zero, later percolated through the Islamic world to Europe, where the Italian mathematician Fibonacci championed them in a treatise published in 1202. Even then, acceptance was sluggish; some merchants and officials were wary of the new numerals, fearing that they were easier to (B) ____ than Roman ones.

Buying secondhand was once associated with thrift or even penury. Today, resale apps make it effortless to sell an unwanted jacket or a used phone within hours. The market for secondhand goods has expanded briskly, notably among younger shoppers. Advocates hail this as a step toward a circular economy, in which products remain in circulation for as long as feasible rather than being discarded. Governments have begun to <u>nudge</u> consumers in the same direction. In 2024 the European Union adopted a directive bolstering consumers' right to have goods repaired, and it agreed to prohibit large companies from destroying unsold apparel and footwear. Skeptics caution, however, that easy resale can also fuel overconsumption: if shoppers know they can readily resell what they buy, they may simply buy more.

Between the 1880s and the 1910s, the Scottish-American industrialist Andrew Carnegie bankrolled the construction of more than 2,500 public libraries around the world, most of them in the United States. Carnegie, who had grown up impoverished and schooled himself by borrowing books from a local man's private collection, fervently believed that libraries offered ordinary people a ladder of self-improvement. His gifts, however, came with stipulations. A town that wanted a Carnegie library had to furnish the land and promise to pay for the building's upkeep with public money every year. Carnegie reasoned that a community which paid for its own library would esteem it, whereas an outright gift might be (A) ____. The program was not without detractors. Some workers resented accepting largesse from a man whose steel mills paid meager wages and had been the scene of a violent strike. A few towns spurned his money altogether.
Yet the buildings outlived the controversy; many still stand, some repurposed as museums or community centers, and several generations of readers have <u>made use of</u> them, often oblivious to the bargain that put them there or to the arguments it once provoked. Whatever one's verdict on the man, his libraries helped make free public reading an (B) ____ part of civic life.

sanguine 은 '낙관하는, 자신만만한'이라 upbeat(낙관적인)와 가까워요. 매출이 줄었는데도 곧 이익이 돌아온다고 장담했다는 뒤 내용이 단서예요. solvent(빚 갚을 능력이 있는)는 회사 재무를 말하는 같은 화제 낱말일 뿐 태도가 아니고, obsequious(아첨하는)는 뜻이 달라요. disconsolate(낙담한)는 반대예요.

Secondhand shopping is now popular only among elderly consumers.
Making resale easier may not by itself reduce overall consumption.
Resale apps typically charge sellers higher fees than traditional shops do.
Young shoppers spend less on new clothing than their parents did.

회의론자들은 쉽게 되팔 수 있으면 더 많이 살 수 있다고 경고했어요. 그러니 'Making resale easier may not by itself reduce overall consumption.'을 끌어낼 수 있어요. 'only among elderly consumers'는 '특히 젊은 층'이라는 글과 어긋나는 단정이고, 앱 수수료와 세대별 옷 지출은 글에 없어요.
Which pair of words best fills in blanks (A) and (B)?
(A) whereas 로 '제 돈을 낸 마을은 아낀다'와 대비되니 공짜 선물은 '방치될(neglected)' 수 있다는 말이에요. (B) 건물이 지금도 서 있고 여러 세대가 썼으니 공공 독서를 시민 생활의 '없어서는 안 될(integral)' 부분으로 만들었다는 결론이에요.
Which of the following is closest in meaning to the underlined expression?

Which of the following would be the most suitable title for the passage?
Why Public Libraries Are Closing Today
Carnegie's Libraries: Generosity with Strings Attached
The Rise of the American Steel Industry
